Every plant in my flat has survived at least one drawing session, and at least one of them has survived my watering habits only by luck.

This little page started next to a tin of paints and a jar of pens: a leaf, then another leaf, then the pot, then the shadow the pot throws on the table. Houseplants are the most patient models you will ever find. They do not move, they do not get bored, and every leaf is a tiny lesson in how light bends around a curve. My favourite trick: draw only the outline of the darkest leaves first, and let the light ones stay almost empty paper. Suddenly the plant has depth. I made a list of thirty plants to draw, one a day, from a monstera to the sad plant in the corner that everyone has. The full list is on my website.

Penguins look like they were designed by someone who already knew they would end up in a sketchbook.

Two ovals, a little beak, two flat feet, and you have a character. Give it a scarf and it has a story. Give it a cup of cocoa and it has a whole winter evening. I wrote down thirty small cozy things a penguin could do: knitting, ice skating, waiting at a bus stop, taking a selfie, falling asleep on a book. The illustration on the card is one of my New Year pictures, the kind of party I actually like, in pyjamas, with snacks and good company. That is the mood I wanted for the list too. One tip if you try it: keep the penguin the same every day and change only what it is doing. By day ten you will know your character by heart, and that is the moment drawing gets really fun. The full list is on my website.

A sewing basket is a treasure chest that nobody thinks of as a treasure chest.

Spools in five colours, a tape measure that never rolls back properly, buttons from coats that no longer exist, a thimble that fits nobody. Every object in there has a different shape and a different shine, which makes it perfect practice. Metal scissors want hard edges and one bright line. Thread wants soft stripes. Buttons are just circles with two or four tiny holes, and drawing thirty of them is strangely calming. I made a list of thirty things you might find in a sewing basket, from a pincushion to a cat lying on the fabric you were about to cut. The painting on the card is from one of my sketchbook spreads, paints and all. The full list is on my website.

I have never met a teapot that was boring to draw.

Round ones look friendly, tall ones look serious, chipped ones look like they have stories, and every single one has that spout, which is the hardest and the most fun part. The painting on this card is one of my sketchbook watercolours of an old town with spires and roofs. It reminded me of all the teapots I have seen in windows of small cafés there. So I wrote thirty teapots to draw: a glass one with tea leaves floating, a cat-shaped one, a teapot in a knitted cosy, a teapot family, and finally your own. A small trick for the spout: draw it as a cone first, then bend it. Do not fight the shape, just tilt it. The full list is on my website.

Snowy fields are where foxes become visible. All summer they are hiding, and then winter puts them on a white page for you.

The watercolour on this card is one of my quiet winter landscapes: bare trees at the edges, a pale field, a little warm orange in the distance. While I was painting it I kept thinking that a fox would fit right in the middle, one orange dot in all that grey. So I wrote a list of thirty foxes in the snow: sleeping, jumping, wearing a scarf, carrying a lantern, reading a book by the fire. The trick with a fox on snow is to keep the snow almost untouched and let the shadows be blue, not grey. Then the orange glows on its own. The full list is on my website.

My kitchen tools all have personalities. The whisk is always nervous, the kettle is always a little sleepy, and the egg cup is shy.

This sketchbook page is a breakfast spread: a teapot, bowls, toast, the whole morning on paper. Drawing it, I realised how much character is already in everyday objects. A ladle looks lazy if you tilt it, a rolling pin looks proud if you stand it up. Add two dots and a tiny mouth and they come alive. I made a list of thirty kitchen tools with faces, from a grumpy whisk to a salt and pepper duo who have been married for years. Draw them small, all on one page, and you will have the funniest sketchbook spread of the week. The full list is on my website.

Trains are my favourite drawing studio. You get a seat, a window, and strangers who stay still for exactly twenty minutes.

The sketch on this card is one of those train drawings: quick ink lines, someone half asleep, no time to think, only to look. Winter trains are even better. The windows fog up, the fields outside turn into long white stripes, someone always has a thermos and someone is always knitting. I wrote down thirty things to draw on a winter train ride, from a ticket and a sandwich to the moonlit lake you see for three seconds before a tunnel. Tip from experience: draw people from behind or from the side, it is less awkward and the shapes are clearer. The full list is on my website.

Some days the only correct thing to draw is something sleeping.

So I made a list of thirty sleepy animals to draw. They are wonderful practice, because sleeping bodies are simple shapes: one big curve, a tucked head, closed eyes as two short lines. You can tell a lot about a person by the shoes at their door.

Muddy wellies say garden. Ballet flats say city. Felt boots say a very cold winter and a very warm grandmother. My sketchbook page on this card is from a walk with a blue sky and branches against buildings, and on the way back I kept looking at people's shoes instead of the sky. Shoes are great drawing practice because they are curved, they have laces and soles and wrinkles, and every pair looks different from every angle. I made a list of thirty boots and shoes to draw, from snow boots to a single lost shoe on a bench. Start with the sole as a long bean shape, then build up. The full list is on my website.

Bowls are just ellipses, steam is just a few soft lines, and colour does all the work: orange pumpkin, deep red borscht, green peas, golden broth. That is where the list came from: thirty trams, buses and little trains to draw, from a steam train to a night bus to your daily ride. Vehicles look scary to draw, but they are only boxes with circles. Draw the box in perspective, add wheels, then windows, then one person inside, and it becomes a story. A lit window at night, a frosty window in the morning, a round attic window, a shop window full of cakes, a window with a cat who owns the street. Some colours you just do not expect to find in your own painting. This acid lime was one of them.

The palette on this card comes from a small detail of my snail Mr Chew in a wizard hat, stirring a cauldron that is bubbling with something very green and very suspicious. Around it everything is dark: ink black, slate, a deep aubergine. That is why the lime glows so much. Light colours are only bright next to dark ones. I pulled eight colours out of this one corner of the picture, with their HEX codes, so you can paint your own magical scene with exactly the same glow. My trick: keep 80% of the picture dark and quiet, and give the bright colour only one small place. The palette is on my website, one click copies the HEX.

Breakfast can be a very dramatic event if you paint it big enough.

Nothing happened today. I sketched it anyway.

That is the secret of keeping a sketchbook: you do not wait for something special to happen. You draw your sock, your cup, your bathroom, and a year later those pages are more precious than any holiday photo. Ordinary days are most of our life, they deserve to be drawn. 1804:
Paint the light first. The shadows will find their way.

This line is about watercolour, and maybe a little bit about life. The photo on this card is from an evening of painting outdoors under a street lamp, where the light was the only thing worth painting. In watercolour you cannot add light at the end, so you protect it from the start: the white paper is your brightest colour. Plan where the light is, keep it clean, and the darks will come by themselves, layer after layer. Free lessons about light and watercolour are on my website.

This is my desk at night: a lamp, a screen, a string of lights, and somewhere a cup of tea going cold. The hardest part of drawing is always the first line. After that, it is just one more line, and one more. I wrote this sentence for the evenings when I do not feel like starting. Make the tea, open the sketchbook, and just begin with something small: the cup itself, the lamp, your own hand holding the pencil. Ten minutes is enough. The paper is patient.
